narrative:
The model estimated a 94.6% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because your law school application was tied to that forecast, the admissions decision treated this as a very high risk of not passing, and your application was rejected.

The strongest factor was your third-year class-standing decile. At 1.00, you were far below the average of about 5.79 among accepted students, and this pushed the prediction strongly toward bar-exam failure. The second most influential factor was your first-year class-standing decile. At 1.00 versus an accepted-student average of 6.00, it also pushed toward failure. Together, these academic-standing indicators outweighed the main factor working in your favor: your LSAT score of 36, which was only slightly below the accepted average of 37.18 and pushed the prediction toward passing, but not enough to offset the concern raised by your class standing.

To move forward, ask admissions for specific feedback and whether an appeal or conditional pathway is possible. Consider retaking the LSAT after structured preparation, strengthening your academic record through additional coursework or a post-baccalaureate program, and providing context for your first- and third-year rankings. Reapplying after demonstrating improvement, or applying to programs with conditional admission and bar-preparation support, would give you a clearer path to show that the risk can be addressed.
